subject: Job Search CRM & AI Application Tailoring Center
question: How much does it cost to run AI resume tailoring and fabrication checks on a live deployment using Claude Sonnet 4.6?
test: Tracked real LLM API calls and total cost recorded in the application's llm_usage_logs database table across live job applications as of 2026-09-15.
decision: Claude Sonnet 4.6 was set as the code default because paying roughly 8.5 cents per application delivers meaningfully better tailoring and fabrication-check quality than free LLM options.
chart_title: Measured LLM Costs and Usage on Live Deployment
detail: Data was pulled directly from the live application's llm_usage_logs table on 2026-09-15.

subject: FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center
question: Which model should decline risky loan applications: Random Forest or XGBoost?
test: Both models were trained on the same features and scored on the same held‑out 20% of the synthetic loans; each declines every application it scores at 0.80 or more likely to default.
decision: The Random Forest goes to production: it has the higher ROC AUC and the higher precision when it declines an application.
detail: Both runs are logged to MLflow.

subject: FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center
question: Which fraud rules can be trusted on their own?
test: Each rule flags card transactions based on amount, time, location and customer only; alerts were scored against the planted fraud that the rules never read.
decision: The velocity rule is exact on this data; amount spikes are kept as a review signal, and together the three rules catch every planted fraud case.

subject: FinTech Credit Risk & Fraud Command Center
question: Is the scoring API fast enough to sit in an application flow?
test: POST /api/predict was called 200 times on a laptop with the model loaded once and cached; CI fails if the median latency reaches 100 ms.
decision: The model is loaded once at startup and cached instead of per request, and the latency limit is enforced in CI.

subject: AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits
question: Does daily retraining after the first drift alert recover model accuracy?
test: Compared untouched model vs daily retraining over the rest of the 60‑day simulated run after the first drift alert (day 40).
decision: Retraining on delayed labels is triggered by the drift alert, cutting accumulated loss by 0.326 and ending at 0.83 accuracy.
detail: Baseline accuracy before the drift was 0.9988 and the first alert fired on day 40.

subject: AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits
question: How much review effort is saved by using the audit_alerts table?
test: Counted days and alerts read versus reviewing every daily metric on the 60‑day simulated run.
decision: Reviewer works from the audit_alerts table, reviewing only 21 days and 25 alerts instead of 60 days and 300 metric values.

subject: AI Model Observability & Fairness Audits
question: Can drift alerts detect accuracy loss without outcome labels?
test: Monitored KS p‑value and PSI on simulated drift starting day 31; recorded first alert day and accuracy changes (simulated data).
decision: Alert fires without needing outcome labels, enabling early detection of accuracy degradation.
detail: The KS alert first fires on day 40, the same day accuracy has fallen 5 points.

subject: Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine
question: Which detection layer finds the injected anomalies: the model or the tax-rate rule?
test: Each layer was scored on its own against injected anomalies in a synthetic general ledger of 1,200 seeded entries.
decision: The rule's flags go first in the review order, and the model and Benford's Law rank the rest.
chart_title: Detection Layer Precision and Recall Comparison
detail: The model layer combines Benford's Law first-digit deviation (30% of the risk score) with an Isolation Forest (70%) and flags entries at a risk score of 65.

subject: Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine
question: How much review work does the priority order save?
test: Entries were opened in priority order (rule hits, then risk score) and, separately, in ledger order on synthetic ledger data, counting how many must be opened to reach 90% of the injected anomalies.

results.label: Priority order entries opened for 90% anomalies
Ledger order entries opened for 90% anomalies

decision: Review starts with the rule hits, then goes down the risk score (review_effort in models/audit_detection.py), and the comparison is recomputed on every run.
chart_title: Entries Opened to Reach 90 Percent Anomaly Detection
detail: Working down the priority order allows an auditor to find 90% of anomalies after opening 43 entries instead of 1,108.

subject: Tax Anomaly Audit Compliance Engine
question: Should validation run row by row or as column operations?
test: The same validation checks were run both row by row and as column operations on 100,000 synthetic entries.

results.label: Row by row time to validate

subject: Real-Time IoT Telematics & Predictive Maintenance
question: Do rolling Z-scores catch sensor spikes without flooding the fleet with false alarms?
test: Simulated fleet telemetry (5 devices, 11,315 readings) with 214 planted sensor spikes; rolling Z‑score (50‑reading window) threshold 3 applied to battery‑temperature and motor‑vibration readings.
decision: The same rolling Z‑score with a threshold of 3 is used for both sensors; alerts repeat at most every 4 hours while a condition persists, resulting in 404 maintenance alerts for the month.
detail: Alerts built on these flags repeat at most every 4 hours while a condition persists.
